newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia premier tight-lipped on cabinet new line-up.
newsitem.headline: Russia premier tight-lipped on cabinet new line-up.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and his new first deputy, Anatoly Chubais, have kept Russia and the world guessing about plans for a cabinet shake-up but promise it will make government more effective.

And President Boris Yeltsin's risky decision to place Chubais, a hate figure for conservatives, in the cabinet appears to have met only half-hearted condemnation from the communist-dominated State Duma or lower house of parliament.

"The president decided to go further then just intentions and took practical steps to reorganise the government," Chubais, Yeltsin's former chief of staff, told a meeting of lawers -- his first public apparance in the new cabinet post.
Yeltsin, in his state of the nation address last Thursday, blasted the government for failing to tackle economic and social crisis in Russia and ordered Chernomyrdin to reorganise the cabinet.
On the next day he named Chubais, who had kick-started Russian privatisation in 1992 and spearheaded Yeltsin's successful re-election campaign last summer, to the government.
Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday the new cabinet, which he had promised to present later this week, will be younger and more professional.
"Professional market economists, firm supporters of the president's course of reforms, will come into the government," Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying.
He added that most new ministers will be under 50 with administrative experience.

"Now there are all possibilities of forming a united and effective team of serious and responsible professionals," Chernomyrdin said, adding personnel changes could be announced sooner than the seven-day deadline set by Yeltsin on Tuesday.
The Duma responded with an angry resolution condemning the nomination of Chubais but stopping short of attacking personally Yeltsin.

In a resolution approved by a thin majority of 230 votes after the second voting, the 450-seat chamber denounced the government policies as "ruinous" and branded Chubais' appointment as a "challenge" to the legislature.

But the deputies made clear they wanted to take part in the shuffle, urging Yeltsin to hold consultations with parliament, and many of them were quick to stress that there was no word about any attempt to topple Chernomyrdin.
"We are not stoking passion, it is just another document similar to those which the Duma had passed before," a leader of the Communist faction Anatoly Lukyanov told NTV commercial television.
The new government will face its first challenge on March 27, when trade unions plan to hold a nationwide day of strikes to protest against long delays in the payment of wages and pensions.
Union leaders said on Wednesday the government changes would not change their plans.
